title: ACME Corp - POC scoping: latency & throughput SLOs
summary: POC scoping to align on success criteria for latency and throughput SLOs. Customer cares about interactive TTFT for chat features and sustained TPOT for batch summarization. Discussed target p95/p99 numbers, workload sizing (concurrency, qps, token distribution), measurement plan (bench harness, warm cache vs cold, synthetic vs replay), and timeline for a 3-week POC with benchmarks and handoff. Next steps: share benchmark spreadsheet, schedule lab access, run smoke test, and provide security docs.
topics: Define TTFT vs TPOT and which matters per workflow
p95/p99 targets for interactive and batch use cases
Workload sizing: concurrency, qps, token length distribution
Benchmark methodology: warm/cold, KV cache, batching, model variants
transcript: [00:00] Jordan Patel: Good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
[00:08] Carlos Ramirez: Hey Jordan, Carlos here, head of ML at ACME. Priya and Tom are on too.
[00:14] Priya Singh: Hi all, Priya, platform, nice to meet you.
[00:18] Tom Baker: Tom, CTO, glade to be here.
[00:23] Jordan Patel: Awesome. Maya from our infra team will lead through latency/throughput scoping. Maya?

[00:28] Maya Chen: Hi everyone. goal today is to align on success criteria for the POC—specifically TTFT versus TPOT, p95/p99 targets, and how we'll measure them. we'll also scope workload size and timeline.

[00:45] Carlos Ramirez: perfect. quick context — ACME is building a customer chat assistant. we need interactive latency under a threshold otherwise UX suffers. we also run nightly batch summarization jobs that care about throughput and cost.

[01:00] Priya Singh: also key constraints: most traffic is short prompts (10-60 tokens) but summaries are 800-1,200 tokens. expected peak concurrency 120 concurrent sessions, baseline steady qps ~80, burst to 250 for campaigns.

[01:20] Maya Chen: ok that's helpful. so two primary workflows: interactive chat (short prompts, TTFT-critical) and long-run summarization (TPOT-critical). let's define terms: TTFT = time to first token — how fast user sees first response; TPOT = time per token (sustained generation speed) — affects cost and tail latency for long outputs.
[01:42] Tom Baker: we've seen vendors quote low TTFT but then token time is high which kills throughput. we'd like clear p95/p99 for both.
[01:50] Jordan Patel: right. to propose realistic targets — what's your current baseline?
[01:55] Carlos Ramirez: our in-house endpoint: TTFT p95 ~480ms, p99 ~820ms for short prompts; TPOT p95 ~12ms/token, p99 ~28ms/token on GPU cluster. we want to get below those while reducing cost.

[02:12] Maya Chen: ok. based on typical SLAs we commonly see for interactive chat: TTFT p95 150-250ms, p99 350-500ms for 10-60 token prompts on optimized infra. for long generation, TPOT p95 6-12ms/token and p99 under 25ms/token depending on model/quantization. are those in scope?
[02:34] Priya Singh: hitting p95 150ms would be massive improvement; p99 under 400ms acceptable. for summarization, p95 8ms/token is great, but we'd accept p95 12ms/token if cost is good.
[02:45] Maya Chen: noted. we should tie success criteria to both latency and quality. you'll want negligible quality regression vs your baseline model. we'll include prompt-set evals as part of POC.
[02:58] Tom Baker: how do you measure TTFT vs TPOT in the bench? we've had confusion before about warm cache vs cold starts.

[03:05] Maya Chen: good point. measurement plan: we'll run four benchmark modes — cold cold (cold worker, cold model), cold warm (warm model but cold KV cache), warm steady (warmed KV cache and warmed compilation), and production-like (with batching and caching enabled). primary measurement will be production-like for SLOs; we'll also report cold/cold for operational visibility.

[03:30] Jordan Patel: and we capture p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT across configured concurrency and qps distributions. we'll replay a traffic trace you provide, and also run synthetic tails to stress p99.
[03:43] Carlos Ramirez: we can provide a 48-hour sample trace anonymized. it has token length histogram and session concurrency samples.

[03:49] Maya Chen: perfect. for workload sizing we need: 1) qps distribution (baseline, peak), 2) prompt length distribution (user vs system messages), 3) long generation jobs characteristics, 4) concurrency targets and acceptable queuing. you gave some numbers earlier — we'll formalize in the spreadsheet.
[04:05] Priya Singh: about batching: we need to balance latency vs cost. can you show tradeoffs?

[04:10] Maya Chen: yes — our bench will sweep batch sizes and concurrency to measure tail latency impact. we'll also test KV prefix caching and prefix reuse to demonstrate cost drop for conversational workloads.
[04:20] Tom Baker: does Redwood support quantized models for cost savings? and how will that affect TPOT?

[04:25] Jordan Patel: we support several quantization profiles; for some models you see 20-40% token throughput improvement and lower GPU memory. we'll include recommended quant profiles per model variant and measure quality delta on your eval prompts.
[04:40] Carlos Ramirez: about models — we may want to test two model families: one higher-quality slower model and one smaller faster variant as fallback. can Redwood route requests automatically?

[04:47] Maya Chen: yes. smart routing can failover to a faster model if latency SLOs are at risk. for the POC we'll test baseline routing and a fallback policy and measure end-to-end user TTFT p99 under simulated capacity constraints.
[05:02] Priya Singh: for p99 we care about tail under load spikes — do you simulate burst traffic?
[05:07] Maya Chen: yes we'll run synthetic burst scenarios and observe p99 behaviour; we'll also track time-in-queue metrics and retries.

[05:15] Jordan Patel: let's outline success criteria we propose now, subject to your sign-off: interactive chat: TTFT p95 <= 200ms, TTFT p99 <= 400ms (production-like bench); summarization: TPOT p95 <= 12ms/token, TPOT p99 <= 25ms/token for 800-1,200 token outputs. Also quality parity: fuzzed ROUGE/BLEU/LLM eval thresholds — we'll put exact numbers in the eval sheet.
[05:44] Carlos Ramirez: those look reasonable. can you also measure 99.9th for TTFT? sometimes our execs ask that.
[05:50] Maya Chen: we can capture p999 but reliability at that tail often correlates with infra-side failures; we'll include it but use p99 as the primary gating metric.
[05:59] Tom Baker: measurement specifics — what tooling do you use for bench?

[06:03] Maya Chen: we use a bench harness based on Locust + custom request replayer that streams tokens. it records TTFT timestamps at server send-first-byte and client receive-first-byte; TPOT measured as per-token send intervals. we'll give you the harness and a runbook.
[06:18] Priya Singh: will you need access to our VPC for private deployment tests?

[06:22] Jordan Patel: for Redwood Private POC yes. for hosted we can run bench from our cloud region against dedicated infra. we'll document required network rules. for ACME, do you prefer a hosted dedicated pool or private VPC?
[06:33] Carlos Ramirez: security team will prefer VPC/private but initially we can do hosted dedicated to move fast. if successful we'll transition to private.

[06:41] Maya Chen: fine. timeline idea: week 0 — kickoff and access; week 1 — bench setup + smoke tests; week 2 — production-like runs and model variant tests; week 3 — final runs, quality evals, and handoff report. roughly 3 weeks total.
[06:58] Tom Baker: what's required from us to start?

[07:01] Jordan Patel: init requirements: 1) anonymized traffic trace (you said you'll provide), 2) a canonical eval prompt set and quality criteria, 3) list of model variants to test, 4) point of contact for infra access (if private).
[07:12] Carlos Ramirez: we'll send the trace and eval set by EOD Wednesday. model list: base-XL (higher quality), base-L (faster).
[07:20] Priya Singh: can you share the benchmark spreadsheet and the bench harness repo?
[07:24] Maya Chen: yes we'll share spreadsheet and a link to the harness. also we'll include instructions to replay your trace and to run warm vs cold profiles.

[07:33] Jordan Patel: regarding reporting — we'll produce a benchmark report with p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, token-cost estimates, CPU/GPU utilization charts, and recommended config (batching, quant, caching).
[07:46] Tom Baker: how do we interpret TPOT for variable-length outputs?

[07:50] Maya Chen: we'll report TPOT as avg ms/token for the generation phase for buckets (short <100 tokens, medium 100-400, long >400). for long summarization we'll specifically report totals for 800-1,200 token outputs and tail behaviour.
[08:05] Carlos Ramirez: make sure the bench accounts for system messages and few-shot context — our typical prompts include 3 system messages totalling ~60 tokens.
[08:12] Maya Chen: will do. also we'll test prefix caching / KV reuse; that usually improves TTFT for chat dramatically when prefix reuse is high.
[08:22] Priya Singh: any recommendations for acceptable warmup time before measuring production-like SLOs?

[08:27] Maya Chen: yes — run a 15-30 minute warmup at your target qps to warm kernels and KV caches, then run steady-state measurement windows of 15 minutes and capture tails. we'll also run several windows to ensure stability.

[08:40] Jordan Patel: risks to call out: 1) cold start and auto-scaling effects on p99, 2) model compilation variance, 3) network variability if hosted across regions. we'll document mitigations like keep-warm footprints and precompiled kernels.
[08:55] Tom Baker: pricing — can you estimate cost per 1M tokens at measured TPOT?
[08:59] Jordan Patel: we'll include cost estimates in the report based on observed throughput and our pricing tiers; for POC we'll run cost sims for both quant and float configs.
[09:08] Carlos Ramirez: ok next steps then?

[09:12] Jordan Patel: propose next steps: 1) Redwood to share bench spreadsheet and harness link, 2) ACME to send trace + eval prompts, 3) schedule lab access or confirm hosted dedicated, 4) run initial smoke test, 5) week 2 full runs, 6) deliver report. we'll capture actionable items now.
[09:34] Priya Singh: sounds good. one more question — do you surface per-token cost breakdown by model route?
[09:38] Maya Chen: yes our console will show per-route token cost and latency breakdowns; we'll include screenshots in the final report.
[09:46] Tom Baker: thanks, I think that's it from us.
[09:50] Jordan Patel: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a proposed kickoff slot for Monday. bye all.
[09:57] Carlos Ramirez: thanks. bye.
